prompt: A cutaway, diagram-style illustration of a machine that is nothing but text. At its center sits the model: a huge sphere woven from billions of fine threads (the "large" of its name), eyeless and handless, with no pockets for keys or bank cards — a ribbon of words flows into one slot and out of another, and that is all it ever touches. Above it, a colossal funnel pours books, newspapers and web pages into the sphere, while a magnifying-glass inset shows the single lesson being drummed in: "The cat sat on the ___," with the machine's pencilled-in guess, "mat." Below, the outgoing ribbon fans out into speech bubbles — a poem, a translation, a tidy summary, a friendly chat reply, a worked logic proof — under the caption "one humble trick, many seeming talents." One bubble declares in confident bold type that the Moon is made of cheese, while a small, plain picture of the real Moon beside it says otherwise; and the input slot is a narrow glowing frame that holds only the newest stretch of ribbon, earlier words trailing away beyond it, faded and unread. Bolted around the sphere like a clearly separate, detachable exoskeleton hangs the agent kit — mechanical hands, a camera eye, keys, a credit card and a clipboard of instructions — labeled "the model alone reads and writes text; wrapped in tools, it becomes an agent."
